title: TB7-12003
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX (the Appellant), a citizen Turkey, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying his claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (the Appellant), a citizen Turkey, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying his claim for refugee protection. He has submitted new evidence in support of his appeal. The Appellant is requesting an oral hearing. The Appellant asks the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to overturn the decision of the RPD and to find that the Appellant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. In the alternative, the Appellant requests that the matter be returned to the RPD for a new hearing under a differently constituted panel.

The Appellant is a long time follower of the Hizmet or Gulenist movement in Turkey (30 years). Since 2007, the Appellant was a member of a charity trust (Mutevelli) which was a Hizmet charity. The Appellant, along with the other members, would decide weekly which Hizmet institutions would receive funding from the charity. As part of the Hizmet group, the Appellant travelled to many different countries to visit Hizmet schools. The charity also established a bursary for university students.

The Appellant also collected donations for the well-known XXXX XXXX Foundation which is a Hizmet affiliated aid organization. The Appellant traveled throughout Turkey during the "Festival of Sacrifices" on behalf of XXXX XXXX to distribute meat to the poor. The Appellant held bank accounts in the Gulenist Bank Asya and was a subscriber to the Gulenist newspaper "Zaman" and the Gulenist magazine, "Sizinti", both of which have been closed by the government because of the Hizmet affiliation.
The Appellant's construction company was negatively impacted by the government's witch hunt as people fearing the government began avoiding doing business with Hizmet related businesses.
The Appellant was a member of the Cerkezkoy Ergene Industrialist Businessmen Association (CESIAT) which was a Hizmet affiliated organization.1

After the attempted coup in Turkey on July 2016, the Appellant fled to Ukraine where he started a business in the hopes of waiting out the problems in Turkey. When the Appellant's visa expired and he was threatened with deportation, he fled to the USA as he had a valid visa for the USA, and two weeks later crossed into Canada where he claimed refugee protection. RPD's Reasons

In its reasons, the RPD found that the Appellant was a follower of Hizmet while acknowledging that the Appellant's son was enrolled at a Gulenist school in Toronto. The panel accepted that the Appellant had been actively promoting and donating to the Hizmet movement and was a member of the well-known Hizmet charity, Kimse Yok Mu. The panel also accepted that the Appellant held bank accounts at Bank Asya (Hizmet bank) and held subscription to two Hizmet publications.
The panel, however, found that the Appellant did not have the requisite subjective fear and did not hold the profile of the type of Hizmet supporter being persecuted by the Turkish government.

Pursuant to section 111(1)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD sets aside the determination of the RPD and substitutes its determination that the Appellant is a Convention refugee. Appellant's Issues

The Appellant raises four issues at the RAD: a. The Member's analysis of the Appellant's lack of subjective fear was unreasonable. b. The Member ignored or failed to assess relevant documentary evidence. c. The Member failed to properly consider if the Appellant meets the threshold of section 96 of the IRPA. d. Does the Appellant have a sur place claim? ANALYSIS Determinative Issue
The determinative issue in this appeal is the Appellant's profile as an active member of the Hizmet or Gulenist movement. Standard of Review
For questions of fact, mixed fact and law, and law, I have applied the standard of correctness as per Huruglica.2 Admissibility of New Evidence
The Appellant submitted new evidence with his Appeal.

Section 110(4) of the IRPA provides that the person who is the subject of the appeal may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of his claim or that was not reasonably available, or that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented at the time of the rejection of his refugee claim.

If the proposed new evidence does meet the requirements of section 110(4), I must then apply the analysis set out in the Federal Court of Appeal's decision in Raza3 as subsequently modified by the same court's decision in Singh; effectively I will assess the credibility and relevance of the evidence in order to determine whether it is admissible.

The Appellant submits one item as new evidence. The item is a newspaper article published on May 21, 2017, two weeks before the RPD decision was rendered. Without good reason, this is not an acceptable item as section 110 (4) of the IRPA makes it clear that the evidence must arise after the decision of the RPD UNLESS it was not reasonably available to the Appellant OR the person could not have reasonably expected to present the evidence at the time of his hearing.

Counsel for the Appellant (counsel) argues that the article was published only two weeks before the decision of the RPD and was an "online publication" which the Appellant only found online in early June. Given the requirement to have the document translated into English (or French), the article was not reasonably available to the Appellant prior to the decision being rendered by the RPD.

I disagree with counsel. The article was online on May 21, 2017 and was available for anyone looking, to find. The fact that the Appellant failed to look for it until sometime in June and then had to find a translator does not make the document "not reasonably available" to him. He could have found the document, if he was looking for it on or about May 21, 2017 when it was published. The Appellant could then have made a request to the Member to make a late submission, requesting time for translation. I have no evidence of these things being done. I have no reasonable explanation sufficient enough to allow me to ignore the provisions of the statute (s. 110 (4)) and consequently, the request to submit this document as new evidence should be dismissed. However, in reading the document, I find that it is highly probative and capable of changing the findings in this claim. Out of the interests of justice, I find that I must allow this article into evidence and do so.

I find that there is no good reason to hold an oral hearing as there is sufficient evidence available to me to make a decision. Therefore that application is dismissed. Arguments Counsel argues that the panel's analysis of subjective and objective fear was unreasonable. Counsel cites Maldonado4 reminding the RAD that there is a presumption of truth unless there be reason to doubt that truthfulness. 1) Counsel reminds me that the panel found that the Appellant lacked fear of persecution in Turkey for two reasons. For not making a claim in the United States of America5 2) For not claiming refugee protection for his son, who is living in Canada with a valid student visa6

Counsel argues that both of these are unreasonable. The Appellant was credible and testified in accordance with his Basis of Claim (BOC) form with no inconsistencies. Counsel argues that the Appellant's subjective fear has an objective basis and therefore, the Appellant's subjective fear should have been accepted by the panel. Counsel cites Shanmugarajah7 as recently cited in Gnanasundaram8 where the Federal Court of Appeal held that "'it is almost always foolhardy for a Board in a refugee case, where there is no general issue as to credibility, to make the assertion that the claimants had no subjective element in their fear...'" and this case would appear to be no exception.

I concur with counsel that the case law cited above is certainly comparable in circumstances to this case. There have been few, if any credibility concerns as the panel made it clear from the beginning of his decision that what was determinative in this case was the panel's finding that there is insufficient objective basis for the fear alleged by the Appellant.

Counsel has made other arguments in the Memorandum and I have read and digested each one however; with the profile of this Appellant, well established by testimony and supporting documentation, I will now begin my own, independent analysis of the claim, based on the evidence before me.

The profile of this Appellant is similar to that of thousands of other Hizmet supporters. The Appellant is not a major Hizmet leader, educator, publisher, prosecutor, judge, soldier, military officer or police officer. This Appellant is just a "foot soldier" so to speak, a hard working supporter of the movement, involved at lower levels in many aspects of the movement. At one point recently, this profile would definitely be insufficient to make the Appellant a likely target upon return to Turkey. In fact, it was more likely than not that when the Appellant left Turkey, his profile was insufficient to make him a target. However, things have changed and this is where counsel argues a sur place claim.

Counsel argues that the new evidence, which is an article that actually names the Appellant and has a photograph of him, states that the Appellant is a member of the Fethullah Terrorist Organization (FETO) and has fled to Canada. As this article was published in Turkey, it is almost guaranteed that the Turkish authorities have seen it and now, if never before, would be looking for the Appellant who would be considered a member of a terrorist organization.

I take note that NDP item 4.11 supports the Appellant's claim / appeal Item 4.11 clearly says that the Turkish government has called the Gulen Movement, also known as the Hizmet Movement and FETO, to be a terrorist organization. The document goes on to say that "Human Rights Watch" notes that being labelled a terrorist group allows Turkey to apply "overbroad terrorism laws against suspected Gulenists." This document expressly states that the Turkish government's "purge" has gone too far beyond its scope and is now targeting people based on their perceived association with Gulen. The Appellant's association with the many Hizmet organizations including schools, charities, business associations and the Bank Asya is clearly sufficient for him to be targeted as a supporter of the FETO, also known as the Gulen Movement or Hizmet.
Whether or not the Appellant held the necessary profile before coming to Canada, this new evidence clearly shows that now he does hold such a profile.
Further, my considerations in this case should be prospective. I will, therefore, take a closer look at the future for this Appellant should he return to Turkey.

In my independent analysis of this appeal, I have canvassed the evidence and have taken special note that in one of the Board's own documents,9 mentioned above ,the Turkish government has called the Gulen Movement, also known as the Hizmet Movement, a terrorist organization. This document goes on to say that "Human Rights Watch" notes that being labelled a terrorist group allows Turkey to apply "overbroad terrorism laws against suspected Gulenists." This document expressly states that the Turkish government's "purge" has gone too far beyond its scope and is now targeting people based on their perceived association with Gulen.

When I consider the above document, alongside of the news article disclosed as new evidence, there is no doubt in my mind that the Turkish government actually intends on persecuting anyone connected to the Gulenist movement and that this Appellant, (and his family who are not a part of this case), will on a balance of probabilities be a target for the Turkish authorities upon his return. Summary

After a fulsome and independent review of the evidence herein, I find that the panel made one serious error which was the incorrect profile the panel afforded to the Appellant in relation to the serious possibility of persecution should he return to Turkey. This error is sufficiently important to cause me to overturn the RPD's decision and find that this Appellant is a Convention refugee. Disposition The RAD has found that the RPD's decision will not stand.

Pursuant to section 111(1)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, the RAD sets aside the determination of the RPD and substitutes its determination that the Appellant is a Convention refugee.
